sit down.example: When Billy sat down, the boa lifted his head and began to sway.
sit down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sit up.meaning: To move from lying down to sitting.
sit up.example: Otus opened his eyes, sat up and gave Charlie a broad smile.
sit up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

so that.example: I want to go the back way so that no one sees me.
so that.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sort of.meaning: A type of; a little bit.
sort of.example: Charlie gave her a forced sort of grin.
sort of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

spill the beans.meaning: To tell a secret or tell what happened.
spill the beans.example: "So, come on, Charlie, spill the beans."
spill the beans.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stand up.example: Otus stood up and stretched his arms, scraping his knuckles on the ceiling.
stand up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

step back.example: Billy stepped back into his room and closed the door.
step back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

straighten up.meaning: To stand straight again after bending.
straighten up.example: Manfred straightened up, rubbing his back.
straighten up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

swing around.example: Letting his bag fall to the floor, Charlie swung around and searched the line of students behind him.
swing around.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take care of.meaning: To deal with; to look after.
take care of.example: I'm sure you've got a lot to take care of.
take care of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take off.meaning: (1) To remove clothes. (2) To remove something from a place ("Brown took off the chain").
take off.example: Billy took off his pajamas himself and put on the blue velvet suit.
take off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take out.meaning: To remove something from a bag or pocket.
take out.example: The old man took out a pen and a notepad and handed them to Charlie.
take out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take over.meaning: (1) (Of a feeling) To become the strongest thing and control you ("curiosity took over"). (2) To continue something that someone else started.
take over.example: Tancred took over, telling it from his point of view.
take over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the corner of his eye.meaning: (From the corner of his eye) Seeing something at the side, without looking straight at it.
the corner of his eye.example: From the corner of his eye Tancred saw a movement in the room beyond the door
the corner of his eye.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the following day.example: The following day Charlie found an opportunity to tell Billy about Runner Bean.
the following day.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the game will be up.meaning: The secret will be discovered and the trick will end.
the game will be up.example: The game will be up, Manfred Bloor.
the game will be up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the rest of.example: Someone pushed Fidelio aside and Charlie failed to hear the rest of his friend's sentence.
the rest of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

there there.meaning: Kind words you say to calm someone who is sad or upset. It is not about a place.
there there.example: "There, there, Charlie. You look quite upset"
there there.usageNote: Informal. Said in a gentle, kind way.

to her horror.meaning: In a way that shocked and frightened her.
to her horror.example: Emma, following, saw to her horror that the water was now level with the tigers' eyes.
to her horror.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

to his surprise.meaning: In a way that surprised him.
to his surprise.example: To his surprise, the being shuffled out and gently closed the door.
to his surprise.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn away.meaning: To turn so that you are not facing someone.
turn away.example: Maisie turned away and led Benjamin down a dim hallway.
turn away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn into.meaning: (1) To go into a place by turning. (2) To change and become something else.
turn into.example: Without a word, the enchanter suddenly turned into an open doorway.
turn into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn over.meaning: (1) To move something so that the other side faces up, often while searching. (2) To roll your body onto its other side in bed ("He closed his eyes and turned over").
turn over.example: Charlie turned over every mattress, bag, box, moth-eaten blanket, pillow, and suitcase.
turn over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn up.meaning: (1) To arrive; to appear. (2) To make a sound louder.
turn up.example: Maisie was in the kitchen with the volume turned up high on the television.
turn up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

up and down.meaning: (1) Moving up and then down again many times ("jumping up and down in her seat"). (2) Backward and forward.
up and down.example: Uncle Paton paced up and down, pinching his chin and scratching his head.
up and down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wait for.meaning: To stay until someone comes or something happens.
wait for.example: He waited for the familiar tumbling sensation
wait for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wake up.example: He was about to open the door when Charlie woke up.
wake up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

watch out for.example: And people like us have got to watch out for one another.
watch out for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

forms: what on earth is going on
what's going on.example: "What's going on?" said a voice from the stairs.
what's going on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wide awake.example: Wide awake now, Charlie leaped out of bed and flipped on the light.
wide awake.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

with a sigh of contentment.meaning: Breathing out slowly because you feel happy and satisfied.
with a sigh of contentment.example: sat back with a sigh of contentment.
with a sigh of contentment.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

would rather.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

you'd better.meaning: You should (or something bad will happen).
you'd better.example: Catching sight of Benjamin's pursuers, Fidelio said, "You'd better."
you'd better.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pop the question.meaning: To ask someone to marry you.

make an honest woman of.example: He's surely going to make an honest woman of Miss Ingledew.

keep someone posted.meaning: To tell someone the news as it happens.

get the better of.meaning: To defeat someone, or to be too strong for them.
get the better of.example: You won't get the better of me.

in vain.example: have waited on the step in vain.

deal with.meaning: To take care of a problem.
deal with.example: We can deal with that later.

get rid of.meaning: To remove something or make it go away.
get rid of.example: Charlie and the others got rid of him.

at bay.meaning: Held off so that it cannot come closer.
at bay.example: they kept the wolves at bay.

fend for oneself.meaning: To look after yourself without help.
fend for oneself.example: you will have to fend for yourself.

on the verge of.meaning: Very close to doing or feeling something.
on the verge of.example: Benjamin, on the verge of tears.

come to rest.meaning: To stop moving and settle in a place.
come to rest.example: She came to rest on Charlie's arm.

rest one's case.meaning: To say you have finished your argument.

first and foremost.example: Kettle was a blacksmith first and foremost.

hang on.meaning: To wait, or to keep holding.

paragraphs.context: One of his ancestors conversed with ravens that sat on a gallows where dead men hung.
paragraphs.simple: This is from the list of endowed children at the start of the book. Billy's ancestor could talk to ravens. People were afraid of this, so he had to leave his village.

paragraphs.context: Tancred can bring wind, thunder, and lightning.
paragraphs.simple: This is from the list of endowed children. Tancred's ancestor was named after Thor, the god of thunder, and Tancred can make storms.

background.note: An endowed art student with crackling blond hair. He is a storm-bringer: his moods make wind, rain and thunder.

paragraphs.context: At every step, great gusts swept around his long legs
paragraphs.mainIdea: A giant walks through terrible winds.
paragraphs.simple: This prologue happens long ago. A giant walks against the winds of Badlock. They come from every side and tear at his hair and eyes.

paragraphs.context: The giant drew his cloak tight around the boy in his arms.
paragraphs.simple: The giant holds his little boy close. They are walking toward a small hollow with trees and water.

paragraphs.context: he found his son talking earnestly to a boy of around ten years with startling snow-white hair.
paragraphs.simple: In the hollow, the giant finds his son Roland talking to a boy of about ten with very white hair.

paragraphs.context: caused Tolemeo's cloak to sparkle with ever-changing colors,
paragraphs.simple: Tolemeo leads the way. In the torchlight his cloak shines blue, then green, then deep purple.

background.note: Roland's uncle, a son of the Red King. His cloak changes color.
Roland's white-haired cousin, who has a pet raven.

paragraphs.context: "We heard that Count Harken was on his way.
paragraphs.simple: Otus thought his wife Amoret would be safe with her brother Amadis. She had a magic mirror, made by her father, the king, for traveling.

background.note: An evil enchanter from long ago who married Lilith, the Red King's eldest daughter. He hates the Red King's family.
The Red King's good second son, who sailed away to an island in the northwest.
Otus Yewbeam, Charlie's ancestor from 900 years ago, a gentle giant. He married Amoret, the Red King's daughter, and is a prisoner in Badlock.

paragraphs.context: They brought us here to Badlock and for two years we have been imprisoned in one of his many towers.
paragraphs.simple: The count kept Otus and his son in a tower for two years. Three days ago, they escaped when Otus kicked the troll who brought their food.

background.note: Otus Yewbeam's little son.

paragraphs.context: "It was the work of a magician," said Tolemeo,
paragraphs.simple: Tolemeo explains that Mathonwy sent snow to stop the fire. But it was too late to save Amadis and Amoret.

background.note: The Red King's youngest child, a daughter born just before the queen died.
A Welsh magician from long ago, the Red King's good friend.

paragraphs.context: "Take the mirror, Otus Yewbeam," he said sternly.
paragraphs.simple: Tolemeo gives the mirror to Otus. He says that Otus has lost his wife, but he still has his son.

paragraphs.context: The giant recognized Oddthumb, leader of Harken's guards.
paragraphs.simple: Oddthumb is the leader of the count's guards. He is big and gray, and his right thumb is huge and ugly.

background.note: The leader of Count Harken's troll guards in Badlock. He has a huge, ugly thumb.

paragraphs.context: "Save Roland," cried the giant, and he threw the mirror high into the air.
paragraphs.simple: Otus throws the mirror into the air. It shines so brightly that the trolls are blinded for a moment.

paragraphs.context: A joyous smile lit Otus Yewbeam's face,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Otus is happy that Roland is safe.
paragraphs.simple: Otus smiles as he sees his son fly away to safety. In the long, lonely years that follow, he smiles every time he remembers this moment.

paragraphs.context: The giant knew it would be useless to run.
paragraphs.simple: The trolls can see again and run down to the lake. Otus knows he cannot escape. Oddthumb picks up the mirror.

paragraphs.context: "Flames! That's what they call you, isn't it?"
paragraphs.mainIdea: A strange boy speaks to the Flames.
paragraphs.simple: A thin, sickly-looking boy stands in the hall of number nine. He sticks out his tongue at the Flame cats.

background.note: Three magic copper-colored cats, Aries, Leo and Sagittarius, who protect Charlie and the good endowed children.

paragraphs.context: he found his grandmother, his great-aunt Venetia, and Eric still staring up at him.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie closes the window. On the landing, his grandmother, Great-aunt Venetia and Eric are all looking up at him.

background.note: The youngest great-aunt, Grandma Bone's sister. She is vain and makes dangerous enchanted clothes.

paragraphs.context: At this point, a third woman emerged from the sitting room.
paragraphs.simple: A third woman comes out. It is Great-aunt Eustacia, and she is carrying a large, flat object wrapped in brown paper.

background.note: The middle great-aunt, Grandma Bone's sister. She has an iron-gray bun and sometimes sees the future.

paragraphs.context: he could meet the subjects in old paintings, people who had lived centuries before.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie can hear voices from photos and paintings, and he can travel into old paintings. Going into the past is one thing; getting out again is much harder.

paragraphs.context: "Mrs. Tilpin isn't someone you can argue with."
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eustacia did not want the package.
paragraphs.simple: Eustacia says she had to take the package. She says nobody can argue with Mrs. Tilpin.

background.note: Joshua Tilpin's mother. Her first name is Titania.

paragraphs.context: "Even Ezekiel is wary of it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Even Ezekiel is afraid of the painting.
paragraphs.simple: Eustacia says the school will not keep the package. Ezekiel says it pulls his thoughts away, like a magnet.

background.note: Dr. Bloor's very old, evil grandfather. He lives in the west wing of the academy and uses dark magic.

paragraphs.context: He could feel it already: a light, insistent tug,
paragraphs.simple: Charlie opens the cellar door. He feels a light pull drawing him down the wooden steps toward the painting.

paragraphs.context: This was not how it should happen.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie has not finished unwrapping the painting when its dreadful landscape starts to fill the cellar. Usually Charlie tumbles into a painting, but this time it is different.

paragraphs.context: He found himself on the lowest step of a stone staircase
paragraphs.simple: Charlie is swung backward through an open door. He is now at the bottom of a stone staircase that winds up into the dark.

paragraphs.context: a black shape capped with steep turrets.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A dark castle on the mountain.
paragraphs.simple: Night is falling. Near the top of the tallest mountain there are red lights and a black building with tall, pointed towers.

paragraphs.context: his best friend, Benjamin Brown, a small, tow-haired, anxious-looking boy,
paragraphs.simple: A few minutes after Charlie goes into Badlock, Benjamin crosses the road to number nine with his dog, Runner Bean.

background.note: Charlie's best friend, who lives across Filbert Street. He is not endowed and goes to a different school.
Benjamin's big, friendly yellow dog. He often helps Charlie and his friends.

paragraphs.context: Benjamin saw that a white moth was hovering around the lightbulb.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Benjamin goes down to the painting.
paragraphs.simple: In the cellar, a white moth flies around the light and then disappears. Benjamin walks to the painting. Runner Bean follows, panting and whining.

paragraphs.context: the yellow dog became a smaller, paler version of himself.
paragraphs.simple: Runner Bean stands in front of the painting as if he is listening. He howls, and then he becomes smaller and paler before Benjamin's eyes.

paragraphs.context: Charlie's Uncle Paton would provide an answer.
paragraphs.simple: Benjamin feels bad about leaving Runner Bean in the painting. He hopes Uncle Paton will know what to do.

background.note: Charlie's great-uncle, Grandma Bone's brother. He hides from daylight because his endowment makes lights burst. He helps Charlie.

paragraphs.context: part of him was missing. The dog part.
paragraphs.simple: Benjamin walks up the road without Runner Bean and feels that part of him is missing. In this city strange things happen, and that worries him.

paragraphs.context: The door was opened by Fidelio Gunn, a violin in one hand and a bow in the other.
paragraphs.simple: Benjamin goes to the Gunns' house. Fidelio opens the door with his violin and bow and asks where Charlie is.

background.note: Charlie's first friend at Bloor's Academy, a music student from a big musical family. He is not endowed.

paragraphs.context: "What a surprise! Can't believe my eyes!
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Gunn greets Benjamin with a little song that rhymes. She asks where his big dog is.

background.note: Fidelio's musical mother. She likes to sing what she says.

paragraphs.context: "He's surely going to make an honest woman of Miss Ingledew.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Gunn talks about Uncle Paton.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Gunn thinks Uncle Paton should marry Miss Ingledew. To "make an honest woman of" someone is an old phrase that means to marry her.

background.note: Julia Ingledew, the kind owner of a bookshop near the cathedral. Uncle Paton likes her very much.

paragraphs.context: He was always rushing into situations without thinking them through.
paragraphs.simple: Benjamin feels angry with Charlie for doing something so risky. Charlie often rushes into things without thinking.

paragraphs.context: Here, there were even more books than in the store itself.
paragraphs.simple: The room behind the bookshop is full of old books from floor to ceiling. They smell musty, but the smell is comforting.

paragraphs.context: Olivia looked quite spectacular in an oversized sweater
paragraphs.simple: Emma and Olivia run toward the others with baskets. Olivia wears a big sweater with "star" written on it in gold sequins.

background.note: A quiet art student with long blond hair. She is endowed: she can turn into a bird and fly.
A lively drama student at Bloor's who loves wild clothes and colored hair. She becomes one of Charlie's best friends.

paragraphs.context: "The Pets' Cafe has been closed," wailed Emma.
paragraphs.simple: Emma says the Pets' Café is closed for good. Through the window they saw Mr. Onimous sitting with his head in his hands.

background.note: Orvil Onimous, a small furry-looking man who runs the Pets' Café and does pest control with the Flame cats.
A café on Frog Street run by Mr. Onimous. Only people with pets are allowed in.

paragraphs.context: "I feel so guilty," he told the giant,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie feels bad about Runner Bean.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie goes back to the giant's room. He feels guilty, because Runner Bean is out there alone and has seen him.

paragraphs.context: "Only Fidelio isn't really normal," Charlie added.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie tells Otus about his life.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie tells the giant about his father, his gift, his great-aunts and his friends. He says Fidelio is a music genius.

background.note: Dr. Bloor's son and head boy of Bloor's Academy. He is endowed: he can hypnotize people. He is cruel to Charlie.
Charlie's grandmother, his father's mother. She was born a Yewbeam. She is cold and bossy and spies on Charlie.
The old, gray boarding school where Charlie studies music, art or drama. Endowed children must go there.

paragraphs.context: Otus led the way down the tower.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Otus and Charlie go down the tower.
paragraphs.simple: Otus carries a candle in an iron dish, and it makes big shadows on the walls. At the outer door he stops and listens.

paragraphs.context: From inside one of the dog's ears, a white moth fluttered out.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moth comes out of Runner Bean's ear.
paragraphs.simple: Runner Bean howls at the giant's sad voice. Then a white moth flies out of his ear and lands on Charlie's arm.

paragraphs.context: "Claerwen," breathed Charlie. "My wand."
paragraphs.simple: Charlie says the moth's name, Claerwen, and calls her his wand.

background.note: A magic white moth that helps Charlie. Her name means 'snow white'.

paragraphs.context: He landed with a light bump on the cold cellar floor of number nine Filbert Street.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie is back in the cellar at number nine. He runs up the steps and hears people arguing above him.

paragraphs.context: It was as if the painting reached out and sucked me in.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie tells his friends what happened.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie explains that he only opened the painting a little, and it pulled him in. He hardly traveled at all.

paragraphs.context: "What will happen to Runner if the trolls want his fur?"
paragraphs.mainIdea: Benjamin is worried about Runner Bean.
paragraphs.simple: Everyone listens quietly to Charlie's story. Then Benjamin asks softly what the trolls might do to his dog.

paragraphs.context: were great admirers of Fairy Tilpin (as they liked to call her).
paragraphs.simple: Dorcas and the Branko twins spend Saturday afternoons in a basement room with Mrs. Tilpin. They used to call her "Fairy Tilpin", but she has changed since she began to talk to Harken.

background.note: A plump, cheerful-looking endowed girl at Bloor's Academy.
A strange new boy with paper stuck in his hair. He is endowed with magnetism: things and people are drawn to him.

paragraphs.context: she reached under the table and produced a gleaming, jewel-framed mirror.
paragraphs.simple: Joshua's mother shows the children a shining mirror in a jeweled frame. She says it is the Mirror of Amoret.

background.note: An ancient magic mirror that once belonged to Amoret, the Red King's youngest child. In cb05 someone uses it to free a shadow from a painting.

paragraphs.context: Is this what happened when you gave in to witchery?
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Tilpin was once blond and pretty. Now her hair is lank, her eyes have dark rings, and her lips are thin. The girls wonder if this is what witchcraft does to you.

paragraphs.context: A vaporous green cloud was rising from the mirror
paragraphs.mainIdea: Green mist rises from the mirror.
paragraphs.simple: Billy looks at the table nervously. Green mist rises from the mirror, and everyone watches it with wide eyes.

background.note: A small white-haired orphan who lives at Bloor's Academy. He is endowed: he can talk to animals.

paragraphs.context: Long after his friends had left, Charlie still wandered the house.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie looks at Runner Bean in the painting.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie walks around the house and goes down to the cellar. He looks at Runner Bean's image in the painting, and the dog's brown eyes seem to blame him.

paragraphs.context: "I'm trying to get you out of there, Runner," Charlie would murmur,
paragraphs.simple: Charlie tries to rescue Runner Bean, but someone has made a barrier between them. Charlie cannot get through it.

background.note: A magician-king who came out of Africa long ago. All the endowed children are descended from his ten children.

paragraphs.context: Charlie omitted most of the details about Badlock
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie tells Mrs. Brown part of the story.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie tells Mrs. Brown about Runner Bean. He leaves out most of the details about Badlock and does not say that a giant saved him.

background.note: Benjamin's parents. They are private detectives and are almost always busy with their work.

paragraphs.context: I know our houses are built on ancient battlefields,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Brown knows the city is strange.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Brown says that strange things happen in this city that no one can explain. It is hard for normal people like her and Mr. Brown.

paragraphs.context: The Pets' Cafe was a favorite meeting place for Charlie and his friends.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The friends will miss the café.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie cannot imagine what they will do without the Pets' Café, or what Mr. and Mrs. Onimous will do without customers.

background.note: Onoria Onimous, Mr. Onimous's tall, gentle wife with a very long nose. She makes the cakes at the Pets' Café.

paragraphs.context: a knight on a white horse, red feathers streaming from his silver helmet,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie thinks of the Red Knight.
paragraphs.simple: Manfred is trying to hypnotize Charlie, and Charlie's head starts to sink. Then he sees a picture in his mind: a knight on a white horse with a shining sword.

paragraphs.context: Billy often wandered up to the ruined castle in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy goes to the ruined castle.
paragraphs.simple: Billy feels safe inside the red stone walls of the old castle. He feels that the Red King and his queen might still be near.

paragraphs.context: Finding Cook was not as difficult as Charlie had imagined.
paragraphs.simple: Cook is having tea in the blue cafeteria with Dr. Saltweather, the white-haired head of music.

background.note: The white-haired head of the music department at Bloor's Academy. He teaches brass and choir.
The cook at Bloor's Academy. She is kind to the children and secretly helps Charlie and his friends.

paragraphs.context: He was head of music and felt responsible for Charlie's lack of progress.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie is not good at music.
paragraphs.simple: Dr. Saltweather, the head of music, is worried about Charlie. Charlie's father is the cathedral organist and a brilliant musician, but Charlie has none of his talent.

paragraphs.context: "There are certain people in this city who've been just waiting to finish off the Pets' Cafe."
paragraphs.simple: Cook says that some people in the city want to close the Pets' Café. They do not like the children meeting there and making plans.

paragraphs.context: It wasn't until the end of homework that Charlie began to miss his moth.
paragraphs.simple: The moth often disappears for a few hours. But in the evening she usually comes back and sits on Charlie's arm or shoulder.

paragraphs.context: He wondered if someone had poisoned him.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie stands in the bathroom feeling dizzy and sick. The room spins around him, and he wonders if someone has poisoned him.

paragraphs.context: Charlie heard a voice screaming in the courtyard below the dormitory.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie jumps out of bed and runs to the window. Other boys are already looking out.

paragraphs.context: The headmaster, Dr. Bloor, opened one of the windows above Manfred's study.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dr. Bloor shouts from a window.
paragraphs.simple: The headmaster opens a window and shouts, asking what is going on.

background.note: The head of Bloor's Academy. A big, stern man with small black eyes. He is Manfred's father.

paragraphs.context: The bus meandered around the city while children jumped off at their stops
paragraphs.simple: The bus goes slowly around the city in the dusk. The streetlights are on, but the narrow alleys are still dark.

paragraphs.context: Gabriel lived on the Heights, a steep cliff road that overlooked the city.
paragraphs.simple: Gabriel usually gets off first, at the bottom of the cliff road where he lives. Today he stays on until the street that leads to the Pets' Café.

background.note: An endowed music student. He can feel other people's feelings and memories by wearing their clothes. He keeps gerbils.

paragraphs.context: he went inside and slammed his front door.
paragraphs.simple: Benjamin is standing on his front step, looking at Charlie's house. When he sees Charlie, he goes inside and slams the door.

paragraphs.context: She seemed excited about something.
paragraphs.simple: Grandma Bone tells Charlie to set the table. She rocks in her chair, and she seems excited about something.

paragraphs.context: "Poking your nose into other people's affairs.
paragraphs.simple: Grandma Bone does not like her brother's research. She says he is "poking his nose" into other people's business, which means he is too curious about things that are not his business.

paragraphs.context: Of all the houses on Piminy Street, this was the most sinister.
paragraphs.simple: On the way to the Kettle Shop, the boys pass the Stone Shop. Inside, in the dark, there are stone soldiers, horses and dogs.

background.note: Mrs. Kettle's shop on Piminy Street, which sells kettles. Its door knocker is a little bronze kettle.
An old street behind the cathedral where the Kettle Shop stands.
A mysterious knight in a red cloak and a silver helmet with red feathers, who comes to help Charlie.

paragraphs.context: there he was: Eric Shellhorn, Great-aunt Venetia's stepson.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie looks through the window and sees Eric Shellhorn behind a tall figure in a robe.

background.note: Venetia's small, quiet stepson. He is endowed: he can make stone carvings come alive and move.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Kettle was a very large, muscular woman, with a crown of smooth, copper-colored hair.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Kettle is big and strong, with copper-colored hair. She wears blue coveralls and oily leather boots.

background.note: A strong, friendly woman who runs the Kettle Shop on Piminy Street and is Cook's good friend.

paragraphs.context: the blue boa came slithering out of the kettle,
paragraphs.simple: The blue boa slides out of a kettle and coils around Billy's legs. Billy puts it on his shoulders and hums to it, and it answers like a small bird.

background.note: A blue boa constrictor snake that once belonged to the Red King. Its hug makes people invisible.

paragraphs.context: But he could feel whiskers and fur and a long skinny tail.
paragraphs.simple: Something squeaks and pulls Billy's hair. Billy catches it but sees nothing. He can feel whiskers, fur and a long tail.

paragraphs.context: The anvil stood in the center of the room,
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Kettle opens a metal door. The room has brick walls, a stone floor, tools on a beam and an anvil in the middle.

paragraphs.context: Billy crawled under a table, his arms folded tight over his bent head.
paragraphs.simple: The troll crashes into the furniture and knocks kettles to the floor. Billy hides under a table, very frightened.

paragraphs.context: They couldn't possibly leave her in this state.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boys stay to help Mrs. Kettle.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Kettle's shop is destroyed and her window is broken. She can hardly stand, so the boys do not want to leave her.

paragraphs.context: but I'd like to know where that troll has gone.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Kettle asks the boys for help.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Kettle's friends will help her clean up the shop. She asks the boys to find out where the troll went, but to stay safe.
